section_title: Can Israel make God give them victory?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Thus the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now the Israelites went out to meet the Philistines in battle and camped at Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek. 2 The Philistines arrayed themselves against Israel, and as the battle spread, Israel was defeated by the Philistines, who struck down about four thousand men on the battlefield. 3 When the troops returned to the camp, the elders of Israel asked, “Why has the LORD brought defeat on us before the Philistines today? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Shiloh, so that it may go with us to save us from the hand of our enemies.” 4 So the people sent men to Shiloh, and they brought back the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Hosts, who sits enthroned between the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.

5 When the ark of the covenant of the LORD entered the camp, all the Israelites raised such a great shout that the ground shook. 6 On hearing the noise of the shout, the Philistines asked, “What is this loud shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?” And when they realized that the ark of the LORD had entered the camp, 7 the Philistines were afraid. “The gods have entered their camp!” they said. “Woe to us, for nothing like this has happened before. 8 Woe to us! Who will deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with all kinds of plagues in the wilderness. 9 Take courage and be men, O Philistines! Otherwise, you will serve the Hebrews just as they served you. Now be men and fight!”

10 So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and each man fled to his tent. The slaughter was very great—thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell. 11 The ark of God was captured, and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died.

context_lines: After the account of Samuel’s growing recognition, the story turns to war. Israel suffers a defeat in which about four thousand men die. The elders ask why the LORD has allowed this, then decide to bring the ark from Shiloh into the camp. They expect its arrival to save them.

The ark is the ark of God’s covenant, and the LORD is described as enthroned between the cherubim. Yet the elders’ proposal is their own recorded response to defeat; this scene contains no instruction from God to bring it into battle. Hophni and Phinehas accompany it, linking the coming events with the earlier warning about Eli’s sons.

Israel greets the ark with a great shout. The Philistines are frightened and remember reports of the deliverance from Egypt, though they speak of gods in the plural. Their alarm does not end the battle: they urge one another to fight rather than become servants.

The second defeat is worse. Thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers fall, the ark is captured, and both of Eli’s sons die. Their shared day of death answers the sign announced in [1 Samuel 2:34](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_samuel/2.htm). The ark’s presence has not guaranteed the outcome the elders expected.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/), [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/4.htm) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm) read the elders’ action as misplaced confidence in an outward sign of God’s presence while failing to face their wrongdoing. They distinguish trusting God from expecting possession of the ark to compel His help. That reading concerns the use made of the ark here; it does not require dismissing the ark’s God-given place in Israel’s worship.

The opening sentence leaves a smaller question for interpreters: does Samuel’s word include a command to fight? [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) understands it that way. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm) discusses that possibility alongside the spread of Samuel’s teaching and prophecy. The verse states that Samuel’s word reached Israel and that Israel went to battle, without reproducing a command to launch this campaign.

The Philistines’ speech also needs to remain their speech. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) acknowledges that their recollection may confuse details of Israel’s history. Their fear shows that the reports of God’s power have reached them; it does not make every detail they say a fresh statement by the narrator about where the Egyptian plagues occurred.
god_plan_lines: The danger of presuming on spiritual privileges also appears in [1 Corinthians 10:1–13](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/10.htm). Paul recalls Israel’s shared deliverance, food and drink, yet warns that these gifts did not make rebellion harmless. He identifies Christ as their spiritual rock and urges his readers to heed the warning.

Paul is speaking about the wilderness generation, rather than directly explaining this battle. The shared lesson is that God’s gifts are not permission to ignore Him or a means of controlling Him. The larger story calls people to depend on His faithfulness while turning from the conduct He condemns.
